title: Mindfulness of death
hook: the Buddha asks his monks how they recall death, and the answers shrink from a day to a single breath

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Montaigne, who hoped to be found planting cabbages. Your line was learn to die. Now Buddhist voices begin.

A hall built of brick, and a group of monks seated before their teacher. The Buddha asks them a direct question: do you practice mindfulness of death? Yes, says one, and explains how. Yes, says another, and explains differently. As they go around the room, something odd happens. The span each one names gets shorter and shorter, from a whole day, to a meal, to a mouthful, to a single breath. The Buddha listens to all of them, then tells them which ones have understood.
screen: `DO YOU RECALL DEATH?` → `EACH ANSWER GETS SHORTER.` → `DOWN TO ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Maranasati is Pali: marana, death, and sati, mindfulness. In this discourse the Buddha says that when it is developed, it brings great fruit and leads toward the deathless. Second, the long spans. The first monk thinks: if only I might live one more day and night, I could attend to the teaching and do much. Another says the same about a single day. Another, as long as it takes to eat one meal. Another, while he chews and swallows a few mouthfuls of food. The Buddha's verdict is quiet but firm: they are living heedlessly. Their mindfulness of death is too slow. Third, the short spans. One monk says: just for the time it takes to chew and swallow one mouthful. Another: just for the time between breathing in and breathing out, or breathing out and breathing in. These two, the Buddha says, are heedful, developing mindfulness of death keenly. Fourth, why the breath. The point isn't fear. It's attention. A day feels long enough to put things off. A breath doesn't. If you only count on this breath, the next unkind word, the next put-off apology, the next thing you meant to notice, is happening now or not at all. The Buddha tells the monks to train this way: we will live heedfully. Some Buddhists today practice this recollection with a short phrase, some simply with the breath.
screen: `MARANA, DEATH; SATI, MINDFULNESS.` · `A DAY, A MEAL: TOO SLOW.` · `ONE MOUTHFUL, ONE BREATH.` · `NOT FEAR, ATTENTION.` · then, large: `THIS BREATH.`

segments.voice: Take one breath as if it were the only one you could count on, not dramatically, just fully: the cool at the nose, the rise of the chest, the long breath out. Then the next, the same way, and if the mind jumps ahead to later today, come back to this breath. If the idea of a last breath feels heavy right now, drop it and simply attend to each breath as it comes.
Maranasati: Pali for mindfulness of death, practiced in the Buddha's teaching down to the span of a single breath. Today's word.
Your line: this breath. Not fear, but attention, one breath at a time. Day seven hundred sixty-four, done.

howItsDone: Some Buddhists practice maranasati, mindfulness of death, as a regular recollection: some repeat a short reflection that life is uncertain and death is certain, others simply attend to each breath as if it were the one they can count on.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: maraṇasati, mindfulness of death (also written maraṇassati).

trapdoor: what you thought: mindfulness of death means dwelling on dying.
what it means: recalling that only this breath is certain, so you live heedfully now.
what a scholar hears: Anguttara Nikaya 6.19, where the spans shrink from a day to one breath and only the shortest are called heedful.

chat.says: Isn't Buddhist mindfulness of death just a way to scare yourself?
options: The point is attention, not fear: count only on this breath, and live heedfully.
Yes, the Buddha praised the monks who were most afraid of dying.
It means planning a whole day ahead, in case it's your last one.
chat.meaning: In this discourse, monks who recalled death across a day or a meal were too slow; the mouthful and the breath were heedful.

notes: AN 6.19 paraphrased (the early English translations of the Anguttara are not on the validator's list). Check the setting (the Brick Hall at Nadika), the order of the monks' answers, the 'four or five mouthfuls' span rendered here as 'a few mouthfuls', and the verdict that only the mouthful and the breath are heedful.
'leads toward the deathless' renders amatogadha, amatapariyosana; Buddhist reviewer to confirm.
Original: मरणसति (maraṇasati); the canonical compound is often maraṇassati. Confirm the Devanagari and the pronunciation guide.
Earlier days of this path (14, 125) named maranasati in passing; this day teaches the sutta itself.
Editor: cut the sweeping 'the same sati that runs all through Buddhist practice' and the hook's closing 'Today:' formula.

Audit: the match game had two identical right-hand answers ('heedless, too slow' for both the day and the meal), making it unanswerable as a matching task; pairs now marana/death, sati/mindfulness, one more day and night/heedless, one breath/heedful.
